attributes.typical_evidence: Review records showing identified access issues and remediation dates
attributes.pass_criteria: DESIGN & TYPE I (as of a date): PASS if issues identified in the most recent review show remediation, meaning access removed or adjusted, completed within the entity's defined timeframe; if no issues were identified, pass by default. FAIL if identified issues carry no remediation process. TYPE II (over the period): PASS if every issue identified across the period's reviews shows remediation completed within the defined timeframe, or no issues were identified; an isolated remediation completed slightly late in an otherwise responsive practice is an exception, not a gap; systematic failure to remediate identified issues, or remediation routinely outside the defined timeframe, is a gap.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A flagged over-permissioned account from the last review was removed the same week, evidenced only by a timestamped Slack message from the reviewer confirming the access was revoked, with no formal ticketing system in use.
calibration_examples.reasoning: No over-literalism: a timestamped message confirming remediation is sufficient proof of timely action for a small team without a formal ticketing system. Demanding a specific ticket format when the substance (dated removal within the defined timeframe) is clearly shown is over-literal.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include an actual review record?
Does the record show whether any issues were identified?
For any identified issues, are remediation actions documented?
For any identified issues, does the evidence show remediation within the entity's defined timeframe?

population.alternate_basis: the access review record itself, showing that the review identified no inappropriate access

attributes.text: Access roles are defined and documented
attributes.typical_evidence: Role definitions in identity provider or access control matrix showing role permissions
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Identity provider or access control system shows defined roles with documented permissions per role. FAIL: No defined roles, or roles have no documented permissions.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: An Okta screenshot shows named groups (Engineering, Finance, Admin) each with a description field listing their associated permissions, but there is no separate written 'role definitions' document.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Live system evidence showing defined roles and their permissions passes even without a companion policy document. The identity provider's own configuration is system evidence of documented roles regardless of whether a redundant document also exists.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A submitted 'Future Access Model' project document lists proposed roles and permissions but is marked 'DRAFT - pending implementation' with several TODO placeholders and no adoption date.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A draft or project document is not an adopted configuration. Placeholder text and an explicit draft banner mean the roles described are not yet in force, so this fails until the roles are shown as actually implemented in the system.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show defined access roles?
Are the roles documented with their associated permissions?

attributes.text: Access is assigned through roles or groups (not individual grants)
attributes.typical_evidence: IdP group assignments or access control configuration showing role-based assignment
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: IdP configuration shows access assigned through roles or groups for the majority of users. Individual grants, if any, are documented with justification. FAIL: Access is primarily assigned through individual grants without role/group structure. FLAG: More than 20% of access grants are individual (not role-based), flag for CPA review.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: An Okta export shows the large majority of employees assigned access via groups, with two long-term contractors holding individual app grants that each have a documented business justification note attached.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Attribute-boundary discipline: the pass criteria explicitly tolerate a minority of individual grants when documented with justification, so a small number of justified exceptions is not a structural failure. Only access primarily assigned through ungoverned individual grants should fail this attribute.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A client-authored spreadsheet states '95% of access is assigned through groups' with no accompanying identity-provider export or screenshot to substantiate the figure.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A client-authored spreadsheet is not system proof for a configuration claim. This attribute tests actual IdP assignment structure, which requires a system export or screenshot corroborating the stated percentage, not a self-reported figure.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A one-person company: the identity provider and each in-scope system show a single human account holding the owner or administrator role, and three service accounts each scoped to a named function; there are no group assignments because there is nobody to group.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Role based assignment at the size of one user is a defined role held by the one account plus function-scoped service accounts, not a group structure with one member. The attribute fails access that is primarily ungoverned individual grants, and an owner role with scoped service accounts is the opposite of that; do not import a fleet expectation onto one person.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show that access is assigned through roles or groups (not individual grants)?

attributes.text: For each user: role assignments align with job functions, or with documented responsibilities and business need
attributes.typical_evidence: Comparison of users' role assignments against their job titles/functions or documented responsibilities (an access review record or a team roster listing each person's duties counts)
attributes.pass_criteria: DESIGN & TYPE I (as of a date): PASS if all users' role assignments match their job title and function, with no admin roles assigned to non admin personnel and no production access for non technical roles, or, where job titles do not describe all of a person's duties, each user's role assignments match their documented responsibilities and business need (for example a founder who handles billing holds billing administration, or the only engineer holds production access); a team roster listing each person's responsibilities, an access review record or a short written list of duties counts as the documentation. FAIL if roles are assigned with no relationship to job function or documented responsibilities. TYPE II (over the period): PASS if every user has role assignments that align with their job function or documented responsibilities; an isolated over broad assignment later corrected in an otherwise least privilege practice is an exception, not a gap; systematic misalignment, for example a developer holding billing administration with no billing duties or a human resources user holding production shell access with no production responsibilities or business need, is a gap. FLAG: role assignment is plausible but the job function description is ambiguous, flag for CPA review.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A DevOps engineer holds both AWS infrastructure-admin access and read-only billing console access; the job description confirms cost-monitoring duties as part of the role.
calibration_examples.reasoning: No over-literalism: an access grant that falls outside the narrowest reading of a job title still aligns with job function when the job description documents the underlying duty. Verify against the actual documented responsibilities before flagging a mismatch.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: No job descriptions exist. A team roster lists each person's duties: the CEO also handles billing and holds billing administration, the only engineer holds production administration, and a contract designer holds the design tools only.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A roster of each person's duties documents their responsibilities, and every assignment matches them.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include an actual comparison of users' role assignments against their job titles, functions or documented responsibilities, such as an access review record listing each person's role and access (not just a verbal description)?
Does the record show that role assignments align with job functions or documented responsibilities?

attributes.text: Privileged users are inventoried across all in-scope systems
attributes.typical_evidence: Privileged user list per system (admin roles in AWS IAM, GitHub org owners, database admins)
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: A privileged user list per system (admin roles in cloud IAM, org owners in code repos, database admins) covers all in-scope systems. FAIL: No privileged user inventory, or any in-scope system is missing from the inventory.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A live screenshot of the AWS IAM console listing all admin-role users was submitted under a generic file name and initially tagged as a miscellaneous document rather than as system evidence.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Live system screenshots are system evidence regardless of how they were labeled at submission. Judge the content of the corpus, not the filename or tag it arrived with, before concluding the inventory is missing.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A founder-typed spreadsheet lists the names of people believed to have admin access to AWS and GitHub, with no accompanying console export or API pull from either system.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A client-authored spreadsheet is not system proof for a privileged-user inventory. The claim requires an actual export or live capture from each in-scope system, not a list typed from memory.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show that privileged users are inventoried across all in-scope systems?

attributes.text: Each privileged user is authorized and has a documented business need
attributes.typical_evidence: Privileged access justification records or approval tickets
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Each privileged user has a documented authorization record (approval ticket, email, or access request) and a business justification for their privileged access. FAIL: Any privileged user lacks documented authorization or business justification.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A privileged access grant is authorized via a timestamped Slack message from the engineering manager approving admin access for a specific incident-response need, with no formal ticketing system in place.
calibration_examples.reasoning: No over-literalism: an informal but verifiable, timestamped approval record satisfies the authorization requirement for a small team without a ticketing system. The substance is a documented approval carrying a business justification, which is what the attribute tests.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: During the walkthrough interview the IT lead states 'we always approve admin access before granting it,' but no approval record, ticket, or email is provided for any of the privileged users.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never a substitute for documented authorization. Each privileged user needs an actual retrievable authorization artifact, not a general assurance given in conversation.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A solo founder holds the administrator or owner role on every in-scope system. The privileged access inventory names the founder for each system with the justification 'sole operator and account owner', dated and kept with the quarterly access review; no approval ticket exists because there is nobody else to approve.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Authorization for a company of one is a documented record, and the founder's dated written justification for each privileged role is that record. The attribute asks for a documented authorization and a business need per privileged user, which a dated inventory entry naming the role and the reason supplies; an approval ticket from a second person is a form the entity cannot produce and the criterion does not demand.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show that each privileged user is authorized?
Does the system configuration show that has a documented business need?

attributes.text: Privileged activities are logged
attributes.typical_evidence: Cloud audit logs or SIEM showing admin activity logging enabled
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: System configuration (CloudTrail, Azure Activity Log, SIEM, or equivalent) shows logging enabled for admin/privileged actions across all in-scope systems. Logs capture who (actor), what (action), and when (timestamp). FAIL: Logging is not enabled for privileged activities on any in-scope system, or logs do not capture all three fields (who, what, when).

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A screenshot shows CloudTrail enabled at the AWS Organizations management account as an org-wide trail, which by design also logs activity in every member account, but no per-member-account screenshot was separately captured.
calibration_examples.reasoning: No over-literalism: an organization-wide trail configured at the management account level demonstrably covers every member account by design, so a live capture proving that structure passes without a redundant per-account screenshot.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The evidence submitted is a page from the cloud provider's public documentation describing that CloudTrail 'can log all account activity,' with no screenshot of this organization's own trail configuration.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A provider's documentation page is not this organization's configuration. The attribute requires proof that logging is actually enabled in this entity's own environment, not a description of the feature's general availability.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show that privileged activities are logged?

attributes.text: Service accounts are documented with owner and purpose
attributes.typical_evidence: Service account registry or secrets manager inventory with owner and purpose columns
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Service account registry or secrets manager inventory lists each service account with a designated owner and stated purpose. FAIL: Any service account lacks a documented owner or purpose.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A live export from the secrets manager shows each service account's resource tags populated with 'Owner' and 'Purpose' fields, but there is no separate formal service-account registry document.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Live system evidence showing the required fields passes even without a redundant standalone document. The secrets manager's own tagging is system evidence of ownership and purpose regardless of format.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A founder-typed spreadsheet lists each service account with an owner name and purpose description, with no corresponding export from the secrets manager or cloud console to confirm the accounts or fields exist there.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A client-authored spreadsheet is not system proof for a configuration claim. The owner and purpose fields need to be corroborated by an actual system export, not asserted in a self-made document.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show that service accounts are documented with owner?
Does the system configuration show that purpose?

attributes.text: Service account credentials are rotated or have defined expiration
attributes.typical_evidence: Secrets manager rotation configuration, credential expiration settings, or short-lived credentials that expire on their own (for example temporary credentials issued by cloud roles, or tokens with an expiry); or manual rotation records showing rotation by the due dates in the company's own schedule, at least once a year (our audit's own minimum)
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Secrets manager or KMS configuration shows automatic rotation enabled, OR credentials are short-lived or carry a configured expiration, OR manual rotation records show credentials rotated by the due dates in the company's own schedule, at least once a year (our audit's own minimum). FAIL: No automatic rotation, short-lived credential, configured expiration or rotation schedule exists for service account credentials, or manual rotation missed the company's own due date or the yearly minimum.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A secrets manager screenshot shows automatic rotation configured with a rotation Lambda attached to each service credential, but does not show a completed rotation event log or 'last rotated' timestamp.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Attribute-boundary discipline: this attribute passes on automatic rotation being enabled in configuration, not on a rotation having already executed, which belongs to operating-effectiveness testing elsewhere. A screenshot of the rotation configuration being enabled is sufficient at the design stage.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: During the interview the founder states 'we rotate all service credentials every quarter,' but no secrets manager configuration screenshot or rotation policy setting was provided.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never config evidence. The rotation schedule or automatic rotation setting must be shown in the actual system configuration or in dated manual rotation records, not asserted verbally.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: Every service workload uses cloud role credentials that expire after one hour; inspected configuration shows no long-lived access keys for service accounts.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Short-lived credentials that expire on their own meet the check.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show that service account credentials are rotated or have defined expiration?

attributes.text: For each review period: service account review was performed (separate from user access reviews)
attributes.typical_evidence: Service account review records showing last-used dates and removal of inactive accounts
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Service account review records show a review performed within the last 12 months that checked last-used dates and removed or disabled unused accounts. This is distinct from the user access review; a user access review alone does not satisfy it. FAIL: No service account-specific review performed within the last 12 months, or review did not check last-used dates.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The service account review is recorded as a distinct, separately-labeled tab within the same quarterly access-review spreadsheet, showing last-used dates and two disabled unused accounts.
calibration_examples.reasoning: No over-literalism: 'separate from user access reviews' means functionally distinct in scope and method, not housed in an entirely different document or tool. A clearly delineated section that independently evaluates service accounts by last-used date and disables unused ones satisfies the requirement.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include an actual service account review records showing last-used dates and removal of inactive accounts (not just a verbal description)?
Does the record show that service account review was performed (separate from iam-05 user access reviews)?

attributes.text: Network architecture is documented
attributes.typical_evidence: Network architecture diagram showing environments, segments, and connectivity
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Network architecture diagram or document is on file and dated or reviewed within 24 months, showing environments, segments, and connectivity. FAIL: No network architecture documentation, or documentation is dated more than 24 months ago.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: Engineering maintains a living architecture page in the team wiki that diagrams the VPCs, subnets, and data flow between services, reviewed and updated four months ago; there is no separate exported diagram file.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A network architecture document can take any durable form (wiki page, diagram tool, slide) as long as it shows environments, segments, and connectivity and was reviewed within 24 months; don't demand a specific file format. The wiki page is current and complete on substance.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence show that network architecture is documented?

attributes.text: Production is isolated from non-production environments
attributes.typical_evidence: Cloud network configuration, account structure, or network segmentation settings
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: System configuration shows production is logically separated from non-production (separate VPCs/accounts, separate clusters, separate database instances, or equivalent isolation). FAIL: Production and non-production share the same environment without separation.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: An engineer captured a live screenshot of the cloud console showing separate AWS accounts for production and staging, submitted under a generic filename with no explicit lane tag at upload time.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Live system screenshots are system evidence regardless of how they were labeled at submission; judge what the capture shows, not its filename or tag. A plainly separate account structure between prod and staging satisfies isolation.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The client submitted a spreadsheet they typed themselves listing production and staging VPC IDs, with no accompanying console capture or export.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A client-authored spreadsheet is not system proof for a configuration claim. Without a captured export or corroborating system view, the isolation claim is unverified and should be a gap pending an actual console screenshot or export.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show that production is isolated from non-production environments?

attributes.text: Access between network segments follows least-privilege rules
attributes.typical_evidence: Security group rules, firewall rules, or network ACL configuration; on managed platforms with no customer-controlled network, provider-enforced isolation and access rules demonstrating least-privilege paths between all relevant segments
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Security group rules, firewall rules, or network ACL output shows traffic between segments restricted to specific ports and protocols, no 'allow all' rules between segments. FAIL: Any 'allow all' rule between network segments, or unrestricted traffic between production and non-production.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A security group export shows explicit allow rules scoped to specific ports between segments (app tier to database on 5432 only), with no allow-all entries anywhere, but no written narrative explains each rule's rationale.
calibration_examples.reasoning: No over-literalism: a live export plainly showing scoped, non-allow-all rules passes even without an accompanying narrative explaining least-privilege intent. The rules themselves demonstrate the control.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: An engineer stated on a call that production and staging don't share any open network rules, but no security group or firewall export was provided.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never configuration evidence. The segmentation claim needs an actual rules export or screenshot before it can pass.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show that access between network segments follows least-privilege rules?

attributes.text: Boundary protection mechanisms are configured
attributes.typical_evidence: WAF configuration, load balancer settings, firewall rule export, or the hosting platform's provider-enforced ingress restrictions, with evidence the protection is active and bypass paths are controlled
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: System configuration shows at least one boundary protection mechanism (WAF, firewall, security groups, or network ACLs) is configured and in active/enabled state. FAIL: No boundary protection mechanisms configured, or mechanisms are in disabled/bypass state.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A three-person startup runs on a managed hosting platform behind a CDN provider; a screenshot shows the CDN's proxy/WAF toggle enabled on the production domain, with no dedicated firewall appliance in place.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Compensating controls are a legitimate pass path at design stage: a cloud-native boundary mechanism like a managed WAF/proxy satisfies this attribute at this scale. The pass should state explicitly that it rests on the compensating cloud-native control.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The evidence submitted was a screenshot of the CDN provider's public marketing page describing its WAF product, not a screenshot of the client's own zone or domain settings.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A provider's marketing or trust page is not this org's configuration. The entity must show its own dashboard or zone settings with the mechanism actually enabled for its domain.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show that boundary protection mechanisms are configured?

attributes.text: Only required ports and protocols are permitted inbound
attributes.typical_evidence: Security group inbound rules or firewall rule export showing allowed ports
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Security group or firewall inbound rules show no 0.0.0.0/0 (unrestricted) access on non-public ports. Only ports required for public services (80, 443) may have unrestricted source. FAIL: Any non-public port (SSH/22, RDP/3389, database ports, admin ports) allows 0.0.0.0/0 inbound access.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A firewall export shows exactly two inbound rules: port 443 open to all, and port 80 redirecting to 443; no other ports appear anywhere in the rule set.
calibration_examples.reasoning: No over-literalism: a fully captured rule set with only public web ports open is itself proof that nothing else is exposed. Don't demand a rule explicitly stating that admin ports are closed when the complete export shows none exist.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The client typed a note stating that SSH access is restricted to the office IP address; no firewall or security group export was attached.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A client-authored note is not system proof. A port-restriction claim needs an actual firewall or security-group export or console screenshot.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show that only required ports?
Does the system configuration show that protocols are permitted inbound?

attributes.text: External access points are inventoried
attributes.typical_evidence: List of public-facing endpoints, domains, and IP addresses
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: A list of external access points (public-facing endpoints, domains, IP addresses) is documented and maintained. FAIL: No documented list of external access points.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: Engineering maintains an internal wiki page listing every public subdomain and its purpose, last reviewed and updated within the quarter.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Solo/small-team proportionality: a maintained internal list is the proportional artifact for this attribute at this company's size. Existence and currency of the inventory is what's tested, not the specific tool used to produce it.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The hosting provider's public status page, listing the provider's own infrastructure regions, was submitted as the entity's external access point inventory.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A provider's infrastructure page is not this org's configuration. The entity needs its own list of its domains, endpoints, and IP addresses, not the vendor's general infrastructure description.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show that external access points are inventoried?

attributes.text: Remote access requires MFA and encrypted connection
attributes.typical_evidence: VPN or remote access configuration showing MFA and encryption requirements
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Remote access configuration shows MFA required AND encrypted connections enforced (TLS 1.2+ or VPN with encryption). FAIL: Remote access lacks MFA or allows unencrypted connections.
attributes.na_condition: N/A if entity has no remote access capability

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The team uses a device-based zero-trust access tool gated by SSO and MFA with encrypted tunnels, instead of a traditional VPN client.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Compensating controls are legitimate at design stage: a zero-trust access tool enforcing MFA and encryption is equivalent to a VPN for this attribute. State the compensating basis explicitly when passing.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The IT admin said on a call that remote access requires MFA, but no VPN or zero-trust configuration screenshot or export was submitted.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never configuration evidence. The MFA-and-encryption claim needs an actual configuration capture showing both requirements enforced.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show that remote access requires mfa?
Does the system configuration show that encrypted connection?

attributes.text: Physical access to facilities requires authorization before being granted
attributes.typical_evidence: Badge/key card system configuration or physical access request form
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Badge/key card system configuration or access request form shows physical access requires authorization before being granted. FAIL: Physical access is unrestricted or granted without authorization.
attributes.na_condition: N/A if entity has no physical facilities

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The four-person company works out of a shared coworking space with no dedicated leased facility; the coworking operator's badge system gates entry to the building and floor, documented as the client's physical access control.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Solo/small-team proportionality: for a company with no facility of its own, a shared building's badge-gated access is the proportional control. State the compensating basis explicitly when passing.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The office manager said in an interview that a badge is required to enter the building, with no badge system export, access request form, or building management confirmation provided.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never evidence. A physical access authorization claim needs a badge system screenshot/export or an access request form on file.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show that physical access to facilities requires authorization before being granted?

attributes.text: Restricted areas (server rooms, network closets) have additional access controls
attributes.typical_evidence: Separate badge reader or lock configuration for restricted areas
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Configuration or documentation shows restricted areas (server rooms, network closets) have additional access controls (separate badge reader, lock, biometric) beyond general facility access. FAIL: Restricted areas use the same access controls as general facility areas.
attributes.na_condition: N/A if entity has no physical facilities

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The office has one shared key-card reader for the floor; the server closet uses a separate physical lock with keys held only by the two engineers, documented in a short internal access note.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Proportional compensating control: a distinct physical lock restricted to a named subset of personnel satisfies additional access controls beyond general facility access, even without a second badge reader.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The facilities lead said restricted areas have extra security without describing what it is, and no documentation or photo of the actual control was provided.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never evidence. The claim needs a description or capture of the actual additional control (lock type, reader, biometric) in place.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show that restricted areas (server rooms?
Does the system configuration show that network closets) have additional access controls?

attributes.text: Physical access is removed when no longer required
attributes.typical_evidence: Offboarding checklist showing badge/key return step, or access system deactivation records
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Offboarding checklist or access system records show physical access revoked (badge deactivated, keys returned) when no longer required. FAIL: No evidence of physical access revocation during offboarding, or devices not recovered.
attributes.na_condition: N/A if entity has no physical facilities

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The offboarding checklist has a line item for badge return and access deactivation, and the two departures logged this quarter both show the box checked with a date, though the checklist template itself hasn't been reformatted in over a year.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Process-exists attributes pass on the existence and use of the process, not the hygiene of its paperwork. A used, dated checklist entry evidencing revocation is sufficient even if the template is old.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence show that physical access is removed when no longer required?

attributes.text: Visitors are identified and logged
attributes.typical_evidence: Visitor sign-in log or visitor management system records, including the building or coworking provider's visitor check-in records, with visitor name, date and host
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Visitor sign-in log or visitor management system records are maintained with visitor name, date, and host. FAIL: No visitor log maintained.
attributes.na_condition: N/A if entity has no physical facilities

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The small office keeps a paper sign-in sheet at the front desk recording visitor name, date, and who they were meeting; it is not a digital visitor-management system.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Proportional form passes: the attribute tests that visitors are identified and logged, not that a specific software system is used. A maintained paper log with name, date, and host satisfies the control.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include visitor sign-in records or a visitor management log?
Are visitors identified in the records (name, date, host)?

attributes.text: Physical access is reviewed at least annually
attributes.typical_evidence: Physical access review record with date and findings, dated within 12 months (our audit's own minimum) or the company's shorter stated interval
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Physical access review record dated within the last 12 months shows review performed with documented findings and follow-up actions. FAIL: No physical access review within the last 12 months.
attributes.na_condition: N/A if entity has no physical facilities

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: Eight months ago the office manager emailed IT confirming who currently holds a badge and flagging two people to remove; the note isn't titled a physical access review and uses no formal template.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Process-exists attributes pass on substance, not on label or template. A dated review of who holds access with documented follow-up action satisfies the annual review requirement even without a dedicated review document.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence show that physical access is reviewed at least annually?

attributes.text: Data at rest is encrypted on all in-scope systems
attributes.typical_evidence: Database encryption settings (RDS encryption status, S3 default encryption, disk encryption config); for a store whose encryption only the provider runs, the provider's SOC 2 report section, published encryption documentation or written answer
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: System configuration output shows encryption at rest enabled on all databases and storage systems containing sensitive data, using AES-256 or equivalent (AES-128 minimum). A store whose encryption only the provider runs, with no encryption setting the company can see or change (such as an email, HR or phone system), is shown instead by the provider's own statement, in its SOC 2 report or published security or encryption documentation or a written answer from the provider, that the company's data is encrypted at rest, naming an algorithm that meets the same minimum. Over a Type II period, that statement is the provider's report covering the period, with a bridge letter for any gap, because the company's own logs cannot show what the provider does inside its service. A store whose encryption the company can see or set in its own console, API or configuration (such as a cloud database, bucket or disk) still needs its configuration output. Reviewing that provider's report is part of the company's dependent vendor review and is judged there. FAIL: Any database or storage system containing sensitive data has encryption at rest disabled, or uses a deprecated algorithm (DES, 3DES, RC4).

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A cloud console screenshot shows encryption enabled on the production database instance and on the storage bucket's default encryption setting, but the capture doesn't separately name the algorithm as AES-256 even though that is the service's documented default.
calibration_examples.reasoning: No over-literalism: when a managed service's encryption toggle is enabled and its documented default algorithm meets or exceeds the minimum, the capture doesn't need to spell out the algorithm name to pass.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The client wrote in a spreadsheet that all databases are encrypted at rest, with no console screenshot or export showing the actual encryption settings.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A client-authored spreadsheet is not system proof for a configuration claim. The encryption-at-rest claim needs an actual console capture or export.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A company that runs no servers cites its HR system provider's SOC 2 report, which states that customer data is encrypted at rest with AES-256. The HR system's admin console has no encryption setting to show.
calibration_examples.reasoning: When only the provider runs a store's encryption and the company has no setting to see, the provider's own statement naming the encryption and an algorithm that meets the minimum takes the place of configuration output. A console capture that cannot exist is never the bar.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A company that runs its own PostgreSQL database on a cloud virtual machine cites its cloud provider's SOC 2 report for encryption at rest, with no capture of the machine's disk encryption or the database's own encryption setting.
calibration_examples.reasoning: The provider's report covers the provider's platform, never a disk or database the company configures itself. Encryption the company can see or set is shown from its own console, API or configuration.

coverage_checks.question: Is data at rest shown encrypted on every in-scope store: by the system's configuration where the company can see or set the encryption, and by the provider's own statement where only the provider runs it?

attributes.text: Data in transit is encrypted using TLS or equivalent for all in-scope connections
attributes.typical_evidence: TLS configuration (SSL Labs report, load balancer TLS settings, API endpoint HTTPS enforcement) for the endpoints on the company's own domains and any TLS setting a provider lets it set
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: TLS configuration output (SSL Labs report, load balancer settings, or API endpoint config) shows TLS 1.2 or higher enforced. SSLv3, TLS 1.0, and TLS 1.1 are disabled. In-scope endpoints are the company's own: its websites, APIs and other endpoints on its own domains, wherever they are hosted, and any TLS setting a provider lets it set, such as a minimum TLS version in a provider's admin console. A server a provider runs for its own service, which the company only connects to (such as a provider's mail, web or sign-in servers), is the provider's and is not tested here, so the protocol versions it keeps open for older clients do not fail this check; reviewing that provider's report is part of the company's dependent vendor review. A company with no endpoint or TLS setting of its own shows this check by scans of the providers' endpoints it connects to, or by those providers' own statements, in their SOC 2 reports or published security documentation or a written answer from each provider, that they encrypt those connections with TLS. Over a Type II period, a provider's statement is its report covering the period, with a bridge letter for any gap. FAIL: Any in-scope endpoint supports TLS 1.1 or below, or SSLv3 is enabled.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A TLS scan of the production API endpoint shows only TLS 1.2 and 1.3 as supported protocols; the report doesn't include a separate line explicitly stating SSLv3 is disabled.
calibration_examples.reasoning: No over-literalism: a scan listing only modern TLS versions as supported IS proof that older protocols are disabled; absence of an explicit negative line item is not a gap.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: Engineering said in a standup that only modern TLS versions are allowed, with no scan report, load balancer configuration, or endpoint capture submitted.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never configuration evidence. The TLS-version claim needs an actual scan output or configuration export.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: Scans of the company's own website and API show only TLS 1.2 and 1.3. A scan of its email provider's mail servers grades B because the provider still accepts TLS 1.0 and 1.1 from older clients.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A server a provider runs for its own service, which the company only connects to, is the provider's and is not tested by this check. The company's own endpoints enforce TLS 1.2 or higher.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show TLS 1.2 or higher enforced on every endpoint on the company's own domains and on any TLS setting a provider lets it set (or, for a company with no endpoint or TLS setting of its own, do scans or its providers' own statements show those connections encrypted with TLS)?

attributes.text: Encryption algorithms and key lengths meet current standards
attributes.typical_evidence: Encryption configuration showing algorithm and key length (e.g., AES-256, RSA-2048+); where only the provider runs the encryption or never shows the algorithm, the provider's SOC 2 report section, published encryption documentation or written answer naming them
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Configuration output shows AES-256 (or AES-128 minimum) for data at rest, RSA-2048+ (or ECDSA P-256+) for key exchange, TLS 1.2+ for transit. Zero deprecated algorithms in use (DES, 3DES, MD5, SHA-1 for signatures, RC4). Each fact is shown from where it lives. A setting the company can see or set (its own endpoints, its own keys, and the encryption on its own databases, buckets and disks) is shown by configuration output. A fact only a provider runs or never shows the company (such as the algorithm behind a provider's default encryption, or the encryption of the company's data in an email, HR or phone system) is shown by the provider's own statement, in its SOC 2 report or published security or encryption documentation or a written answer from the provider, naming the algorithm and key length. Over a Type II period, that statement is the provider's report covering the period, with a bridge letter for any gap, because the company's own logs cannot show what the provider does inside its service. For encryption in transit, a server a provider runs for its own service, which the company only connects to, is the provider's and is not tested here. FAIL: Any deprecated algorithm is in use, or key lengths are below minimum (RSA <2048, AES <128).

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The transit-side TLS scan confirms compliant key exchange and cipher suites, but doesn't separately show a database encryption key length, which is covered by a different attribute's own evidence.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Attribute-boundary discipline: don't import a neighboring attribute's evidence requirement into this one. If the algorithms and key lengths shown for this attribute's scope meet the standard, that is sufficient.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A security questionnaire response stated the company uses strong encryption and modern key lengths, with no actual configuration or scan output attached.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Written self-attestation without a capture is not configuration evidence. The algorithm and key-length claim needs an actual scan or configuration export.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The company's website scan shows TLS 1.2 with RSA 2048-bit keys and AES-GCM suites. Each SaaS provider holding its data states AES-256 encryption at rest in its SOC 2 report, and none offers an encryption setting to capture.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Encryption the company controls is shown from configuration output, and encryption only the provider runs is shown by the provider's own statement of the algorithm and key length.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A storage bucket's console page shows it uses the provider's default encryption keys, and the provider's encryption documentation states those keys are AES-256. The console never shows an algorithm.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Each fact comes from where it lives: the visible setting from the console, and the algorithm the console never shows from the provider's own statement.

coverage_checks.question: Do the encryption algorithms in use meet current standards, each shown by configuration output where the company can see or set it and by the provider's own statement where only the provider runs it or never shows it?

Do the key lengths in use meet current standards, each shown by configuration output where the company can see or set it and by the provider's own statement where only the provider runs it or never shows it?

attributes.text: Cryptographic keys are stored securely (not in source code or plaintext)
attributes.typical_evidence: KMS configuration, secrets manager setup, or code scan results showing no plaintext keys; for keys a provider holds inside its own service, the provider's SOC 2 report section, published encryption documentation or written answer
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Configuration shows cryptographic keys stored in a KMS, secrets manager, or HSM. Code scan results or repository search confirms no plaintext keys in source code or config files. A company with no source code shows that search over the folders and drives where it keeps configuration and key files. For keys a provider holds inside its own service, which the company never handles (such as the keys that encrypt its data in an email, HR or phone system), the provider's own statement, in its SOC 2 report or published security or encryption documentation or a written answer from the provider, that those keys are kept in a key management service or HSM takes the place of configuration. Over a Type II period, that statement is the provider's report covering the period, with a bridge letter for any gap, because the company's own logs cannot show what the provider does inside its service. Keys the company creates, downloads or holds itself (such as a service account key file, a signing key, or a key in its own KMS) still need the configuration and the scan or search above. FAIL: Keys found in source code, config files, or stored in plaintext outside a secrets management system.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A code repository search for common secret patterns shows zero hits, and a separate secrets-manager dashboard screenshot shows the production signing key stored there; the two captures come from different tools rather than one unified report.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Judge the substance across the corpus, not whether it arrives in one unified report. A clean code-scan capture plus a secrets-manager capture together satisfy the attribute.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The engineering lead said on a call that keys are never hardcoded, with no code scan results or secrets manager configuration provided.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never evidence. The no-plaintext-keys claim needs an actual code scan output or secrets manager configuration capture.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The company's SaaS providers state in their SOC 2 reports that the keys encrypting its stored data are kept in a managed key service. The one signing key the company holds sits in its cloud secrets manager, shown in a screenshot, and a repository scan finds no plaintext keys.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Keys a provider holds inside its own service are shown by the provider's own statement; keys the company holds itself are shown by configuration and the scan.

coverage_checks.question: Are cryptographic keys shown stored securely (not in source code or plaintext): by configuration and a code scan or search for keys the company holds, and by the provider's own statement for keys a provider holds inside its own service?

attributes.text: Key rotation is performed or scheduled
attributes.typical_evidence: KMS key rotation settings or key rotation log showing rotation history; for keys a provider holds and rotates inside its own service, the provider's statement of automatic rotation or of its last rotation date
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: KMS configuration shows automatic key rotation enabled, OR manual rotation log shows rotation performed at least annually (rotation date within past 12 months). For keys a provider holds and rotates inside its own service, which the company cannot rotate itself (such as the keys that encrypt its data in an email, HR or phone system, or a provider's default key in its cloud account), the provider's own statement, in its SOC 2 report or published security or encryption documentation or a written answer from the provider, takes the place of KMS configuration when it shows that the provider rotates those keys automatically, or gives the date it last rotated them within the past 12 months. Over a Type II period, that statement is the provider's report covering the period, with a bridge letter for any gap, because the company's own logs cannot show what the provider does inside its service. Keys the company creates, downloads or holds itself still need the configuration or rotation log above. FAIL: No key rotation configured and no manual rotation evidence within the past 12 months.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A KMS console screenshot shows automatic key rotation toggled on for the production key; there is no separate rotation history log showing a completed rotation event yet.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Read the pass criteria precisely: automatic rotation enabled is an independent, sufficient pass path. Don't additionally demand a manual rotation history log when auto-rotation is on.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: An admin said verbally that keys are rotated every year, with no KMS configuration screenshot or rotation log provided.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never configuration evidence. The rotation claim needs an actual KMS config screenshot or a dated rotation log.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The company's cloud storage uses the provider's default keys, which the company cannot rotate itself, and the provider's encryption documentation states those keys are rotated automatically at least every 90 days. The company holds no keys of its own.
calibration_examples.reasoning: For keys a provider holds and rotates inside its own service, the provider's own statement of automatic rotation takes the place of KMS configuration.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The company created a key in its own cloud key management service with automatic rotation off and no rotation record in the past year, and cites the provider's documentation that the provider rotates its default keys.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A key the company creates in its own key management service is the company's to rotate. The provider's statement covers only the keys the provider holds and rotates.

coverage_checks.question: Is key rotation shown performed or scheduled: by KMS configuration or a rotation log for keys the company holds, and by the provider's own statement of automatic rotation or a dated rotation for keys a provider holds and rotates inside its own service?

attributes.text: Data disposal procedure exists
attributes.typical_evidence: Data disposal policy or procedure document covering physical and logical disposal
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Data disposal procedure document describes methods for data wiping (software-based) and hardware destruction (physical) for different asset types. FAIL: No data disposal procedure, or procedure does not describe specific wiping or destruction methods.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The company's asset handling policy has a short paragraph stating laptops are wiped via full-disk encryption key destruction before being recycled through a certified e-waste vendor; there are no other asset types since the company is fully cloud-based with no on-prem servers.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Solo/small-team proportionality: the procedure must be proportional to the entity's actual asset footprint. A short but concrete description covering the only asset type in use satisfies the attribute.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include a data disposal policy or procedure document covering physical and logical disposal?

attributes.text: For each disposed asset: data is wiped or destroyed before disposal
attributes.typical_evidence: Certificate of destruction, data wipe log, or disposal vendor receipt
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: every asset disposed of in the period has a certificate of destruction, a data wipe log, or a disposal vendor receipt. FAIL: an asset was disposed of with no evidence of secure wiping or destruction. An isolated missing certificate in an otherwise documented practice is an exception, not a gap; systematic absence is a gap. If the population was empty for the period, this is not a pass by default: show the place these are recorded, empty, over the period, and record it as non-occurrence. Whether a disposal procedure exists is asked by A1 of this control.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: No laptops or hardware were disposed of during the period; the client has a written disposal procedure on file but no disposal events occurred to test against it.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Absence of disposal activity is a pass-by-default condition under this attribute's own criteria, not a gap. An AI that treats an empty population as an automatic fail is over-conservative; verify there truly were no disposals before failing.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The client stated no assets were disposed of during the period, so no destruction certificates or wipe logs were provided. The asset inventory submitted for the asset control shows six laptops moved to status 'retired' with retirement dates inside the period, plus one line noting a hardware return to the leasing vendor.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A pass by default for a non-occurrence has to be corroborated by the record, never accepted on assertion alone. The entity's own inventory shows disposals inside the period, so the no-disposals branch of the criteria does not apply, and the absence of any wipe log, certificate, or vendor receipt for those six assets is a gap.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include an actual certificate of destruction (not just a verbal description)?
Does the record show that data is wiped or destroyed before disposal?

attributes.text: For each disposal: disposal is documented with date, method, and asset identification
attributes.typical_evidence: Disposal log entries with asset ID, disposal date, and method used
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: every disposal in the period is documented with the asset identification, the disposal date, and the method used. FAIL: a disposal has no record, or the record omits the asset, the date, or the method. An isolated incomplete record in an otherwise documented practice is an exception, not a gap; systematic absence is a gap. If the population was empty for the period, this is not a pass by default: show the place these are recorded, empty, over the period, and record it as non-occurrence. Whether a disposal procedure exists is asked by A1 of this control.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The most recent disposal record shows the asset tag, disposal date, and wipe method used, but the entry lives in a shared internal document rather than a dedicated disposal-log tool.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Process-exists attributes pass on substance, not on the tool that holds it. A shared document entry that includes asset identifier, date, and method satisfies the documentation requirement regardless of what software it's kept in.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include an actual disposal log entries with asset id (not just a verbal description)?
Does the record show that disposal is documented with date, method?
Does the record show that asset identification?

attributes.text: Data retention schedule is defined
attributes.typical_evidence: Data retention schedule document or policy section listing data categories and retention periods
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Data retention schedule document lists data categories with defined retention periods for each. At minimum covers customer data, employee data, and system logs. FAIL: No data retention schedule, or schedule does not define retention periods.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: Retention periods for customer data appear in the main security policy, and retention periods for employee data and system logs appear in a separate HR data-handling addendum; no single consolidated schedule exists.
calibration_examples.reasoning: The substance of a defined retention schedule can live across more than one document as long as each required category is covered with defined periods. Customer, employee, and log retention periods are all present and were reviewed together, so splitting them across a security policy and an HR addendum still satisfies the attribute.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence show that data retention schedule is defined?

attributes.text: Retention periods align with contractual and regulatory requirements
attributes.typical_evidence: Retention schedule with legal/regulatory basis column for each retention period
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Retention schedule includes a legal/regulatory basis or contractual justification column for each retention period. FAIL: Retention periods have no documented basis or justification.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A clean, professional-looking retention schedule defines specific periods for every data category, but has no column or notes citing any legal, regulatory, or contractual basis for those periods.
calibration_examples.reasoning: This attribute adds a distinct requirement beyond a schedule existing: each retention period needs a documented legal, regulatory, or contractual basis. Reasonable-looking periods with no basis column at all satisfy the neighbor attribute (schedule defined) but fail this one, which demands the justification be documented.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence show that retention periods align with contractual?
Does the evidence show that regulatory requirements?

attributes.text: Removable media and endpoint devices are protected
attributes.typical_evidence: MDM configuration showing USB restrictions, or endpoint encryption settings
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: MDM configuration or policy settings show endpoint encryption enabled (FileVault, BitLocker) and removable media restricted or encrypted. FAIL: Endpoints lack disk encryption, or removable media is unrestricted without compensating controls.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: One MDM screenshot shows FileVault enabled on all laptops and a second screenshot from the same console shows USB storage restricted, taken moments apart during the same review session.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Live system evidence counts regardless of whether every sub-clause is captured in a single screenshot. The same console session plainly shows both endpoint encryption and removable-media restriction, so two screenshots from one live source are together sufficient system proof.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: An engineer states in a review call that the team tells new hires verbally not to plug in personal USB drives, but no MDM configuration, policy document, or acceptable-use text was found.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never configuration evidence. A spoken practice with no MDM enforcement and no written policy leaves removable media effectively unrestricted, which is the failure condition for this attribute.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show that removable media?
Does the system configuration show that endpoint devices are protected?

attributes.text: Process exists for deleting or anonymizing data when retention periods expire
attributes.typical_evidence: Data deletion procedure or automated purge configuration documentation; for a manual process, its named owner and, once a retention period has expired, a record of a deletion carried out
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Document describes a process for deleting or anonymizing data when retention periods expire, AND an enforcement mechanism is in place: an automated lifecycle policy or scheduled deletion job that is configured (it passes before any retention period has expired), or a documented manual process with an assigned owner and, once any retention period has expired, evidence of execution. FAIL: Retention schedule exists but no enforcement mechanism (no configured lifecycle policy or deletion job, and no owned manual process), or a manual process shows no evidence of execution although a retention period has already expired.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: An S3 lifecycle policy document describes automatic deletion of customer data after the retention window, configured last quarter; the company has not yet had a case where the window actually elapsed and data was purged.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A process-plus-enforcement attribute passes on a real, configured enforcement mechanism, not on a history of executions that have not yet come due. An automated lifecycle policy that is actually configured and would fire on schedule satisfies the enforcement requirement even with no purge event to point to yet.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The retention policy describes deletion at the end of each retention period clearly and by data category. The cloud console shows no lifecycle rules on the buckets holding the archived permit files, no scheduled deletion job exists, and no owner is named for carrying it out manually.
calibration_examples.reasoning: This attribute requires the process and an enforcement mechanism behind it, so a policy describing deletion with nothing arranged to perform it fails. A manual route can satisfy the enforcement half, but only with a named owner and, once a retention period has expired, evidence it happens, and neither is present here.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A five-month-old company's deletion procedure assigns its operations lead to delete customer records 12 months after a contract ends; no contract has ended yet, so no deletion has come due.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A documented manual process with an assigned owner is an enforcement mechanism; evidence of execution is asked once a retention period has expired.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include a data deletion procedure or automated purge configuration documentation?

attributes.text: Policy addresses local storage of ePHI on endpoints and removable media
attributes.typical_evidence: Data handling or acceptable use policy section on local storage of ePHI
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Policy either prohibits storing ePHI on endpoints and removable media, or requires that any such storage is inventoried, encrypted, and backed up before device movement. FAIL: No policy position on local ePHI storage.
attributes.na_condition: N/A if the HIPAA compliance add-on is not in scope

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The data handling policy prohibits storing production data, including ePHI, on laptops and removable media, with no exceptions.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Prohibition is one of the two accepted policy positions. An inventory of local ePHI storage is only required when such storage is permitted, so failing a prohibition policy for lacking one is wrong.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The acceptable use policy tells staff to 'handle patient data with care' and to 'avoid keeping files locally where possible'. No definite position on local ePHI storage appears anywhere.
calibration_examples.reasoning: An exhortation to be careful is not a policy position. The policy must either prohibit local ePHI storage or set the inventory, encryption, and backup requirements for it; 'avoid where possible' does neither.

coverage_checks.question: Does the policy take a definite position on local ePHI storage (prohibited, or inventoried, encrypted, and backed up)?

attributes.text: Endpoint protection is deployed on all managed endpoints
attributes.typical_evidence: MDM or EDR console showing device count and deployment coverage
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: MDM or EDR console output shows endpoint protection deployed on 100% of managed endpoints, device count matches managed device count. FAIL: Endpoint protection coverage is below 100% of managed endpoints.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: An EDR console export shows 11 of 12 managed devices covered; the twelfth is a laptop already wiped and removed from the active roster per a closed IT offboarding ticket dated before the test date.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Coverage is measured against the true current managed population, not a stale device count. A laptop confirmed decommissioned and removed from service is no longer a managed endpoint, so coverage of the actual current fleet is 100 percent and passes.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The founder states in the interview that 'all our laptops have antivirus installed' but no MDM or EDR console export, device list, or screenshot was provided to confirm deployment.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never configuration evidence. A spoken assurance about endpoint coverage with no system export to inspect cannot establish the 100 percent deployment this attribute requires.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show that endpoint protection is deployed on all managed endpoints?

attributes.text: Disk encryption is enforced
attributes.typical_evidence: MDM encryption policy or FileVault/BitLocker enforcement settings
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: MDM configuration output shows disk encryption (FileVault, BitLocker, or equivalent) enforced as a policy on all managed endpoints, 100% compliance. FAIL: Disk encryption policy is not enforced, or any managed endpoint shows encryption disabled.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: An MDM console screenshot shows an aggregate compliance tile reading '8/8 devices, 100% FileVault enabled' rather than a row-by-row per-device listing.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A live console's own aggregate compliance figure is system evidence of the substance required, full disk encryption enforced across the fleet. An itemized per-device row is not required when the console itself reports 100 percent enforced.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The written security policy states 'FileVault is required on all company laptops,' but no MDM query, console screenshot, or endpoint export confirming the actual enforced state was provided.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A policy statement is not proof of the live configuration it describes. This attribute requires a system capture showing encryption is actually enforced, so a written requirement alone gaps pending real config evidence.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show that disk encryption is enforced?

attributes.text: Screen lock is enforced
attributes.typical_evidence: MDM screen lock policy showing auto-lock timeout (e.g., 5 minutes)
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: MDM or OS configuration shows screen lock enforced with auto-lock idle timeout of 15 minutes or less. FAIL: Screen lock is not enforced, or idle timeout exceeds 15 minutes.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: MDM enforces a 10-minute screen lock timeout on company-owned devices; two contractors use personal BYOD laptops outside MDM enrollment, but a documented BYOD policy requires the same timeout and each contractor has signed an acceptable-use agreement confirming it.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A compensating control is a legitimate pass path when the basis is real and documented. A signed BYOD policy enforcing the equivalent idle timeout stands in for direct MDM enforcement on devices outside the platform's reach, so this passes on that documented compensating basis.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: An onboarding checklist has a manually checked box next to 'enable screen lock' for each new hire, with no MDM policy or system query confirming the actual setting on any device.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A self-attestation checklist is not configuration evidence. Ticking a box during onboarding proves an instruction was given, not that the setting is actually enforced on the device, so it gaps absent a system-level confirmation.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show that screen lock is enforced?

attributes.text: Automatic OS and software updates are enabled
attributes.typical_evidence: MDM auto-update policy, patch management configuration, or each device's automatic update settings, shown for every device, under a written update rule
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: MDM configuration shows automatic OS/software updates enabled, OR a managed patch management process with defined cadence is documented and enforced. FAIL: No automatic updates and no managed patch process for endpoints.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: MDM enforces automatic OS updates, but third-party application updates are handled through a documented monthly patch cadence run manually by IT rather than an automated tool.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Read the full pass criteria before failing: it explicitly accepts a managed patch process with a defined cadence as an alternative to automation. Automated OS updates alongside a documented, enforced monthly third-party patching routine satisfies the attribute rather than failing for not being fully automatic.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: An internal wiki page recommends 'employees should turn on automatic updates,' but no MDM policy, script, or device query confirms the setting is actually enforced anywhere.
calibration_examples.reasoning: An aspirational recommendation is not an adopted, enforced control. A suggestion with no enforcement mechanism or verification leaves the actual patch state unknown, so it gaps pending real enforcement evidence.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show that automatic os?
Does the system configuration show that software updates are enabled?

attributes.text: For each detected threat: investigation and remediation is completed
attributes.typical_evidence: EDR alert records showing investigation steps and remediation actions taken
attributes.pass_criteria: DESIGN & TYPE I (as of a date): PASS if the entity has an endpoint protection process for investigating and remediating detected threats, and the most recent detected threat has EDR alert records showing investigation steps taken and remediation completed. If no threats were detected as of the test date, complete dated EDR detection history through that date must prove the empty population; record non-occurrence. This does not waive the threat investigation and remediation process. FAIL if there is no threat investigation and remediation process, or a recent detected threat has no investigation or remediation record. TYPE II (over the period): PASS if every detected threat in the period has EDR alert records showing investigation and completed remediation; if no threats were detected in the period, complete dated EDR detection history covering the full period must prove the empty population; record non-occurrence; isolated misses in an otherwise working practice are an exception, not a gap; systematic absence of investigation or remediation is a gap.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: An EDR console export covering the full period shows zero detected threats or alerts; no investigation or remediation records exist because nothing was ever flagged.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Read the default-pass clause before failing: the attribute explicitly passes when no threats were detected as of the test date. An empty alert log with no incidents to investigate is a pass, not a missing-evidence gap.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include an actual edr alert records showing investigation steps and remediation actions taken (not just a verbal description)?
Does the record show that investigation?
Does the record show that remediation is completed?

attributes.text: Software installation on production is restricted to authorized personnel
attributes.typical_evidence: Production access list showing restricted install permissions, or CI/CD pipeline config
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Production access configuration (IAM roles, CI/CD pipeline permissions) restricts software installation to authorized personnel only, non-admin users cannot deploy to production. FAIL: Non-authorized personnel can install software on production systems.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A CI/CD pipeline settings screenshot shows only two named accounts hold deploy permission to production; no separate raw IAM policy JSON export was provided alongside it.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A live pipeline permissions screen plainly showing restricted deploy access is system evidence of the control. A second export format is not required when the substance, that only authorized accounts can deploy, is already visible.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The engineering handbook states 'only admins can deploy to production,' but no CI/CD permissions export, IAM policy, or console screenshot was provided to confirm the actual access configuration.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A written policy statement is not proof of the live access configuration it describes. Without a system export showing who can actually deploy, this gaps pending real configuration evidence.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show that software installation on production is restricted to authorized personnel?

attributes.text: Production admin access list is limited and documented
attributes.typical_evidence: Production admin user list with business justification; in a team of one to three engineers, every engineer may hold admin with a documented need for each account, subject to the existing CPA-review flag
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: Production admin user list is documented with business justification for each admin. Admin count is limited relative to total team size. FAIL: No documented production admin list, or admins lack business justification. FLAG: Admin count exceeds 30% of total engineering team, flag for CPA review.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: A system-pulled admin roster shows 3 of 8 engineers hold production admin rights (about 38 percent), each with a documented business justification for the access.
calibration_examples.reasoning: The 30 percent admin ratio is a review trigger, not an automatic fail: the criteria call for flagging ratios above it for CPA attention. A documented, justified admin list above the threshold passes with a note for reviewer attention rather than gapping.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The founder compiles a list of production admins from memory and email searches rather than pulling it from the actual IAM console or access management system.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A client-authored recollection is not system proof of who holds admin access. An admin list is a system-state claim that needs to come from an actual access management export, not a founder's memory, so it gaps pending a real roster.

coverage_checks.question: Does the evidence include a list of production admin accounts?
Is each admin account documented with business justification?

attributes.text: Removable media usage is restricted or governed by policy
attributes.typical_evidence: MDM USB restriction settings or acceptable use policy covering removable media
attributes.pass_criteria: PASS: MDM configuration shows USB/removable media restrictions enforced, OR acceptable use policy governs removable media usage. FAIL: Removable media is unrestricted and no governing policy.
attributes.na_condition: N/A if entity does not use removable media

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: The company has no MDM platform, but its acceptable-use policy explicitly prohibits use of removable media without a documented exception process, signed by all employees.
calibration_examples.reasoning: A governing policy is an explicit alternative pass path here, not just technical MDM enforcement. A clear, signed acceptable-use restriction on removable media satisfies the attribute, so it passes rather than gapping for lacking an MDM setting.

calibration_examples.evidence_summary: An employee mentions in an interview that 'nobody really uses USB drives here,' with no MDM restriction and no written policy addressing removable media at all.
calibration_examples.reasoning: Verbal confirmation is never configuration or policy evidence. An informal spoken habit with neither a technical restriction nor a governing policy leaves removable media ungoverned, which is the failure condition.

coverage_checks.question: Does the system configuration show that removable media usage is restricted or governed by policy?

attributes.text: Software deployments follow the change management process
